node.label: Mariana Valverde
node.date_label: “The Struggles of the Immoral” (with Weir) 1988 · The Age of Light, Soap, and Water 1991 · “Pauperism, Moral Character, and the Liberal State” 1992 · Diseases of the Will 1998 · Law’s Dream of a Common Knowledge 2003
node.description: A sociologist and criminologist, not a historian by training (PhD in social and political thought, York, 1982; University of Toronto Centre of Criminology from 1993); historians read her study of social purity in English Canada as a statement of moral regulation. The Age of Light, Soap, and Water (1991) follows reformers who sought 'to reshape the ethical subjectivity of both immigrants and native-born Canadians' and argues that their movements 'helped to shape the bourgeoisie, which led the movements, as well as the working class'; her notes trace the term to Corrigan and Sayer's The Great Arch but 'restrict the term to mean the formation of ethical subjectivity', and she held, as 'Foucault and his followers have pointed out', that 'the state has no monopoly on moral regulation'. In 1992 she endorsed Mitchell Dean's argument that classical liberalism was 'a particular system of economic, social, and moral regulation' and faulted Jean-Marie Fecteau's account of relief institutions as means of class control as 'a rather functionalist formulation'. Historians used and contested the frame: Tina Loo asked that it 'address Christianity and certainly Protestantism more fully, even if only to dismiss its importance' (1992), Donald Wright found that the reformers' silent audiences gave 'the impression of top-down social control, precisely what Valverde sought to avoid' (1995), and Nancy Christie and Michael Gauvreau wrote that she and Doug Owram 'have adhered to a caricature of the antiquated and esoteric Victorian theologue to excise the churches from “progressive” currents of modern thought and social action' (1996). Later books turn to alcohol and the will (Diseases of the Will, 1998) and to law (Law's Dream of a Common Knowledge, 2003).
node.representative_figures_and_works: Mariana Valverde (b. 1955); “The Struggles of the Immoral: Preliminary Remarks on Moral Regulation” (with Lorna Weir, Resources for Feminist Research, 1988); “Poststructuralist Gender Historians: Are We Those Names?” (Labour/Le Travail, 1990); The Age of Light, Soap, and Water: Moral Reform in English Canada, 1885–1925 (1991; reissued 2008 with a new introduction); “Pauperism, Moral Character, and the Liberal State” (Labour/Le Travail, 1992); Gender Conflicts (ed. with Franca Iacovetta, 1992); Studies in Moral Regulation (ed., 1994); “Deconstructive Marxism” (Labour/Le Travail, 1995); Diseases of the Will: Alcohol and the Dilemmas of Freedom (1998). After 2000: Law’s Dream of a Common Knowledge (2003); “Introduction to the 2008 Edition” of The Age of Light, Soap, and Water. In-period readings: Loo, Dehli and McCormick (reviews, 1992); Wright (1995); Christie and Gauvreau (1996); Strange and Loo, Making Good (1997); Hunt (1997, 1999).
node.scope_note: Read on 2026-10-14: her review essays 'Poststructuralist Gender Historians' (1990) and 'Pauperism, Moral Character, and the Liberal State' (1992) in full, and 'Deconstructive Marxism' (1995) at pp. 329–332; four in-period reviews or review essays of The Age of Light, Soap, and Water in full (Loo 1992, Dehli 1992, McCormick 1992) or in their Valverde section (Wright 1995, pp. 122–126). The book itself is known here only through those reviewers' quotations and through search-within snippets of the 2008 reissue, which keeps the 1991 pagination for the original text (checked: pp. 15, 17, 165 and 166 match the 1992 reviewers' page references; the 1991 preface's p. 9 appears as p. ix). Christie and Gauvreau (1996), Strange and Loo (1997), Hunt (1999) and Diseases of the Will (1998) are known only through such snippets. 'The Struggles of the Immoral' (1988, with Lorna Weir) is unread. She is not presented as the originator of moral regulation: Corrigan (1981) and Corrigan and Sayer (1985) precede her, and she credits their theorization as 'influential here' while finding that it obscures 'the agencies of regulation internal to civil society'. She called herself a sociologist working between disciplines; Loo (1992) and Wright (1995) read her that way, and the 2008 introduction, a later reading, says that 'no history department in Canada would ever hire me'. The 2003 book is cited at title level only; the 2008 introduction is a later reading and carries no claim about the 1990s.

proposed_edges.relationship: Moral regulation as the formation of ethical subjectivity, carried out by philanthropies, churches and professions as well as the state: social purity in English Canada, 1885–1925 (1991–92; the 1988 article with Weir is listed but unread)
proposed_edges.map_label: Light, soap and water: moral regulation, 1991
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Her own in-period statements. 'Pauperism, Moral Character, and the Liberal State', Labour/Le Travail 30 (1992), pp. 213–222, read in full: 'I have argued elsewhere that the discourse of moral reform needs to be analyzed seriously, not merely dismissed as a cover for class interests', though 'moral discourse does as a matter of contingent fact legitimize certain class, gender, and racial interests' (p. 216); she credits Corrigan and Sayer's The Great Arch with pioneering 'the liberal state's role in constituting subjectivities' (p. 217). The Age of Light, Soap, and Water (1991) is known here through in-period reviewers' quotations and through Google Books search-within snippets of the 2008 University of Toronto Press reissue (volume ghqEyXf5950C; partial preview, page images not viewable here because the viewing limit was reached), which keep the 1991 pagination: reformers sought 'to reshape the ethical subjectivity of both immigrants and native-born Canadians' (p. 17; quoted by Dehli 1992, p. 316); purity work 'was not simply a question of banning obscene books or suppressing prostitution but was rather a campaign to educate the next generation' (p. 17; quoted by McCormick 1992, p. 124); the reform movements 'helped to shape the bourgeoisie, which led the movements, as well as the working class' (p. 15; Dehli, p. 318); 'Moral regulation is very closely linked to state formation, as the British school of historical sociology has argued; but as Foucault and his followers have pointed out, the state has no monopoly on moral regulation' (p. 165; snippet, the last clause also quoted by Dehli, p. 317); '[m]oral regulation is an important aspect of ruling, helping to constitute class, gender, sexual, and race relations' (p. 166, as quoted by Wright 1995, p. 124). Her notes, seen only as snippets, place the concept: in The Great Arch 'the role of the state in moral regulation is highlighted, and their theorization has been influential here; but the agencies of regulation internal to civil society are obscured' (n. 34, p. 171); Corrigan and Sayer 'do not differentiate between moral and other modes of social regulation; by contrast, I restrict the term to mean the formation of ethical subjectivity' (p. 173). Note 33 (p. 171) cites the 1988 article with Lorna Weir, which is unread here. In-period reception by historians. Tina Loo (Labour/Le Travail 30, 1992, pp. 277–279, read) calls the book 'a provocative and valuable contribution to the history of social reform and, more significantly, because of its self-conscious use of theory, to the writing of Canadian history' (p. 279). Donald Wright (Acadiensis, 1995, pp. 122–126 read) calls it a 'much talked about treatise' by 'a sociologist' (p. 122) and its concept of 'slippages' among class, gender, sexuality and race her 'most original' contribution (p. 124). Carolyn Strange and Tina Loo's Making Good: Law and Moral Regulation in Canada (1997; Google Books snippets, pp. 5, 63) write that 'Theorists influenced by philosopher Michel Foucault have urged scholars to abandon the social-control model for a more flexible concept of regulation' (p. 5) and cite 'Mariana Valverde and others' on prostitution as 'the social evil' (p. 63). Mary Louise Adams's 'In Sickness and in Health: State Formation, Moral Regulation, and Early VD Initiatives in Ontario' (1994) is cited at title level only. In-period criticism. Loo finds the second argument, on philanthropy and the state, 'more asserted than proved' (p. 279). Kari Dehli (Historical Studies in Education, 1992, pp. 315–319, read) would draw 'not quite so sharply drawn' conclusions about state and civil society and finds that she moves 'quickly from analysis of discursive strategies ... to drawing conclusions about people's motives and intentions' (pp. 318–319). Wright judges her claim that audiences 'knew precisely what was meant' 'untenable' and finds 'the impoverished immigrant and the "fallen woman" ... conspicuously silent', so that 'the silence of the consumer amidst the din of the producer gives the impression of top-down social control, precisely what Valverde sought to avoid' (pp. 125–126). Chris McCormick (Atlantis, 1992, pp. 123–125, read) asks how her interpretations are made and judges that a 'thorough' reading of context is 'optimistic' (p. 123), while agreeing that 'Regulation is a better word than control' (p. 124). Sociologists reformulated the concept: Alan Hunt's 1997 abstract (read) treats moral regulation not as 'a specific moral arena' but as 'a component of all fields of social relations', a wider definition than hers; in Governing Morals (1999; snippets) he writes 'I do not take issue with Valverde's invocation of ethical subjectivity, but I emphasise the mundane features of self-governing' (p. 155). Dean (1994) and Ruonavaara (1997) are cited through their abstracts as on the moral_regulation node. A contribution, not a founding: Corrigan (1981) and Corrigan and Sayer (1985) precede her, and she credits them. Diseases of the Will (1998), on alcohol and the governance of the will, is title-level here (snippets only) and does not support this edge.
proposed_edges.target_strand_note: moral_reform ('Moral reform and social purity'; 'reform as a productive, not only repressive, project') holds her, Weir, Strange and Loo, and lof_valverde_1991; it is exactly the checked claim. governmentality_reformulations also holds her, for Diseases of the Will (1998), which is only snippet-level here.

proposed_edges.relationship: Protestant reformers read as moral regulators rather than as religious actors, and the church historians' objection that this excised the churches from progressive thought (1991–96)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Her object overlaps the field's. The book studies Methodist and Presbyterian church organizations, the Salvation Army, the WCTU, the YWCA and the National Council of Women (Dehli 1992, p. 316, read), with familiar reformers such as Chown, Shearer and Woodsworth (Loo 1992, p. 277, read). Her reading is regulatory: purity work 'was rather a campaign to educate the next generation' (p. 17, quoted by McCormick 1992, p. 124), and the discourse of moral reform 'needs to be analyzed seriously, not merely dismissed as a cover for class interests' ('Pauperism, Moral Character, and the Liberal State', 1992, p. 216, read). In-period objections from historians of religion and reform. Loo (Labour/Le Travail 30, 1992, p. 278, read) finds that 'religion and sectarian differences' get 'rather short shrift', suggests Richard Allen's typology of radical, progressive and conservative reformers, and holds that 'any discussion of the discourse of moral reform in Canada needs to address Christianity and certainly Protestantism more fully, even if only to dismiss its importance'. Nancy Christie and Michael Gauvreau, A Full-Orbed Christianity (1996), known here only through Google Books search-within snippets: 'historians such as Doug Owram and Mariana Valverde have adhered to a caricature of the antiquated and esoteric Victorian theologue to excise the churches from "progressive" currents of modern thought and social action' (p. xiii); 'Valverde has argued that in early twentieth-century Canada issues such as social purity and immigration were controlled by a hegemonic exercise of power by the state and middle-class organizations' (p. 187), and her analysis 'wrongly posits the view that given the hegemonic influence of the state, there was only one option regarding immigration policy – that of racism and the annihilation of immigrant culture', against which they set 'three divergent strands of opinion on the immigration question' among Protestant clergy (p. 188; n. 95, p. 328, cites her pp. 15, 112, 123–8). Their p. 187 summary attributes to her a state-centred hegemony that her own p. 165 qualifies ('the state has no monopoly on moral regulation'); the disagreement is recorded, not adjudicated. A comparison, as her roster row and edge_861 (moral_regulation – cdn_religion_reform) have it: the criticism runs from the church historians to her, and she did not answer it in a text read here. The dispute is person-level, which is why it is drawn from her entry; edge_861 stays the field-level comparison.
proposed_edges.target_strand_note: secularization_comparison ('Comparisons: British secularization and moral reform'; 'Valverde's moral reform is the regulatory neighbour of the social gospel') holds her. The revisionists strand (Christie, Gauvreau, Van Die) holds her critics; it is named here as the source of the objection, not as the target.

proposed_edges.relationship: Liberalism read as a system of moral regulation and the liberal state as a constitutor of subjectivities (1991–92), beside the liberal order framework's later history of property, the individual and rule
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Her own in-period statements, before McKay's prospectus (2000). 'Pauperism, Moral Character, and the Liberal State', Labour/Le Travail 30 (1992), pp. 213–222, read in full, endorses Mitchell Dean's argument 'that classical English liberalism was not a negation of state regulation but rather a particular system of economic, social, and moral regulation', so that 'a history of pauperism is also a genealogy of liberalism' (p. 217). She reviews Jean-Marie Fecteau's Un nouvel ordre des choses (1989) as 'a landmark work' whose 'theoretical sophistication' crosses 'the traditional historiographical boundaries separating coercion from benevolence and the state as a whole from charity' (pp. 221–222), but faults its 'moyens de contrôle' as 'a rather functionalist formulation', a 'model of negative class power', and adds that 'These moral codes are not intrinsic to the logic of capital, since capitalism works quite efficiently in different cultural systems' (p. 222). Note 10 (p. 220) cites Fecteau's essay in Greer and Radforth's Colonial Leviathan (1992), and the essay thanks Allan Greer for comments on a draft (p. 222). In the 1991 book (Google Books search-within snippets of the 2008 reissue, 1991 pagination) note 35 (p. 171) cites Bruce Curtis's 'Preconditions of the Canadian State', and she writes that moral regulation 'might be an important social process, which is intertwined with but is not an effect of either the economic or the political' (p. 165) and that 'one has to be sceptical of any claims that envision a clear separation between moral and economic regulation' (p. 166). Reviewers read the book's state argument in the same terms: private philanthropy 'allowed liberal democratic states to adhere to their policy of non-interference in the private sphere' (Loo 1992, p. 278, her paraphrase). Comparison only. The user decided (2026-10-12) that the liberal order framework is 'a different project closer to history of capitalism'; Fecteau and Curtis are shared ground (state formation), not membership. No in-period text by the framework's authors discussing her was read here (McKay's 2000 prospectus is paywalled and unread). edge_848 (liberal_order_framework – moral_regulation) is the field-level comparison. This edge is an editorial comparison of her 1992 argument with the later framework (McKay, 2000); she did not distinguish herself from a framework not yet formulated.
proposed_edges.target_strand_note: state_formation_roots ('State formation before the framework': Curtis, Greer, Radforth) is the ground her 1991 notes and 1992 essay share with the framework (Curtis; Colonial Leviathan). Fecteau sits in the property_and_capitalism and critiques strands for his 2009 reply, which is later than the 1989 book she reviewed.

proposed_edges.relationship: Scott's poststructuralist programme criticised by a sympathetic reader, who suggested that it may exaggerate what Foucault and Derrida can do for historians, for passing over discourse analysis's bias towards 'the sociology of domination', and (1995) for setting theory against working-class history
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Her own in-period words (1990 essay read in full; 1995 essay, pp. 329–332 read). 'Poststructuralist Gender Historians: Are We Those Names?', Labour/Le Travail 25 (1990), pp. 227–236, reviews Scott's Gender and the Politics of History with Denise Riley's 'Am I That Name?'. She grants that Scott's approach 'has much to commend it' but finds her four elements of gender 'somewhat arbitrary' and asks whether the definition 'finally succeeds in transcending the idealism/materialism dichotomy' (p. 230). Scott's case studies show limitations 'symptomatic of the general limitations of discourse analysis as it has been used by social historians (myself included!)' (p. 231): there is 'an inherent bias in discourse analysis in favour of what some call "the sociology of domination." This problem, not discussed by Scott, does not discredit or make redundant discourse analysis' (p. 232). Scott's 'rather polemical book tends to sing the praises of discourse analysis without mentioning many of its problems', with a 'grandiose claim made by Scott on Foucault's behalf' (p. 232), and 'It may be that she exaggerates the contribution Foucault and Derrida can make to historical work' (p. 233). She ends that 'Scott's work deserves to be carefully read even by those who find some of its more polemical claims hard to swallow' (p. 233). 'Deconstructive Marxism', Labour/Le Travail 36 (1995), pp. 329–340 (pp. 329–332 read), sharpens the judgment: Scott 'made an influential attempt to extend the reach of deconstruction within historical writing to the certainties of class. Her argument was limited in many ways' (pp. 331–332); 'Scott probably used her new-found theories to justify a break with Marxism that she, like so many other former leftists on both sides of the Atlantic, wanted to make anyway', and 'the book undoubtedly made an important contribution to the feminist analysis of both politics and history: but it did so, or at least gave the appearance of doing so, at the expense of working-class history' (p. 332). She criticises the other side too: 'for many labour historians, any hint of theoretical sophistication became prima faciae evidence of political backsliding' (p. 332), and her note names Bryan Palmer's Descent into Discourse as 'the by now standard Marxist critique of Scott' (p. 332, n. 5). edge_891 (joan_wallach_scott → cdn_women_gender) already cites the 1990 essay as evidence of Canadian engagement with Scott; this edge records her own criticism of Scott's position, which edge_891 does not carry. A critique within broad sympathy, not a rejection: the qualifications above are part of the claim.
proposed_edges.target_strand_note: The joan_wallach_scott person entry has no strands. The criticism concerns her 1988 book's claims for poststructuralist discourse analysis.
proposed_edges.include_note: Proposed because the brief asks for critique edges where the person criticised an atlas entry's position in her own words; both essays were read in full or at the relevant pages. edges_considered_not_proposed.reason: Not proposed. She criticises class-functionalist and political-economy accounts of welfare: in 1991 'Marxist accounts (and in Canada this chiefly means accounts produced by the political economy school)' and liberal accounts alike (p. 165, snippets; elsewhere her notes cite Panitch, ed., The Canadian State, 1977, and find in Guest's The Emergence of Social Security in Canada 'a liberal framework', p. 170), and in 1992 Fecteau's 'rather functionalist formulation' and 'the pitfalls of marxist functionalism' (p. 222, read). No atlas entry holds the Canadian political-economy position; a critique of marx would generalise a dispute that she frames inside the left ('one can take moral discourse seriously and still admit' its class effects, 1992, p. 216). Carried in the evidence of edges 1 and 3.

new_sources.citation: Mariana Valverde, “Pauperism, Moral Character, and the Liberal State,” review essay on Mitchell Dean, The Constitution of Poverty (1991), Jean-Marie Fecteau, Un nouvel ordre des choses (1989), and Gertrude Himmelfarb, Poverty and Compassion (1991), Labour/Le Travail 30 (Fall 1992): 213–222.

verification.note: Read in full (pp. 213–222) in the journal's own PDF (lltjournal.ca article 4860, galley 5733; citation line on p. 213: Labour/Le Travail, 30 (Fall 1992), 213-22). Passages used: 'a critique of political economy for its failure to theorize moral regulation and subjectivity generally' (pp. 213–214); 'moral capital of the poor' (p. 215); 'the discourse of moral reform needs to be analyzed seriously, not merely dismissed as a cover for class interests' and 'moral discourse does as a matter of contingent fact legitimize certain class, gender, and racial interests' (p. 216); Dean shows 'that classical English liberalism was not a negation of state regulation but rather a particular system of economic, social, and moral regulation'; 'a history of pauperism is also a genealogy of liberalism'; Dean 'undercuts the Marxist view that moral regulation is an unimportant offshoot of economic class relations by expanding the analysis of the liberal state's role in constituting subjectivities pioneered by Corrigan and Sayer' (p. 217); Fecteau's study 'sadly lacking' Dean's awareness of gender (p. 220); n. 10 on Fecteau's essay in Colonial Leviathan and his perspective 'not to my knowledge otherwise represented in Canadian historiography' (p. 220); 'moyens de contrôle', 'a rather functionalist formulation', 'a model of negative class power', 'the pitfalls of marxist functionalism', 'These moral codes are not intrinsic to the logic of capital', 'a landmark work' (p. 222); thanks to Lynne Marks and Allan Greer (p. 222).

new_sources.scope_note: Her in-period statement of liberalism as moral regulation, and her critique of class-functionalist accounts of relief.

new_sources.title: Mariana Valverde, “Deconstructive Marxism,” Labour/Le Travail 36 (Fall 1995): 329–340.
new_sources.citation: Mariana Valverde, “Deconstructive Marxism,” review essay on Jacques Derrida, Specters of Marx (1994), Labour/Le Travail 36 (Fall 1995): 329–340.

verification.note: Journal PDF (lltjournal.ca article 5013, galley 5882; citation line on p. 329: Labour/Le Travail, 36 (Fall 1995), 329-40). Pages 329–332 read; the rest searched by keyword only. Passages used: 'Joan Scott made an influential attempt to extend the reach of deconstruction within historical writing to the certainties of class. Her argument was limited in many ways' (pp. 331–332); 'Scott probably used her new-found theories to justify a break with Marxism that she, like so many other former leftists on both sides of the Atlantic, wanted to make anyway'; 'Scott's rather exaggerated claims about what great male French theorists can do for feminism'; the book's contribution made 'at the expense of working-class history'; 'for many labour historians, any hint of theoretical sophistication became prima faciae evidence of political backsliding'; n. 5 names Palmer's Descent into Discourse as 'the by now standard Marxist critique of Scott' (all p. 332).

new_sources.scope_note: In-period: her later judgment of Scott and of the discourse debate in Canadian labour history.

new_sources.citation: Tina Loo, review of Mariana Valverde, The Age of Light, Soap and Water: Moral Reform in English Canada, 1885–1925 (Toronto, 1991), Labour/Le Travail 30 (Fall 1992): 277–279. doi:10.2307/25143633.

verification.note: Read in full in the journal's PDF of the issue's reviews section (lltjournal.ca article 4867, galley 5740; pp. 277–279; signed Tina Loo, Simon Fraser University). Crossref gives Labour/Le Travail 30, p. 277. Passages used: the book is 'not a history of events ... but one of meaning' (p. 277); the reformers' allegories taught 'the right type of consciousness' (p. 278, quoting p. 41); 'religion and sectarian differences' get 'rather short shrift'; Allen's typology; 'any discussion of the discourse of moral reform in Canada needs to address Christianity and certainly Protestantism more fully, even if only to dismiss its importance'; private philanthropy 'allowed liberal democratic states to adhere to their policy of non-interference in the private sphere' (p. 278, her paraphrase); the state argument 'seems to be more asserted than proved'; she 'locates her book in the separate, but converging disciplines of history and sociology'; 'a provocative and valuable contribution to the history of social reform and, more significantly, because of its self-conscious use of theory, to the writing of Canadian history' (p. 279).

new_sources.scope_note: In-period review by a historian (later co-author of Making Good, 1997).

verification.note: Read in full (pp. 315–319) from the journal's PDF, an image scan without a text layer, OCR'd locally; quotations checked against the OCR text, not re-checked against the page images. Signed Kari Dehli, Ontario Institute for Studies in Education. Crossref: HSE/RHE 4:2, pp. 315–319, issued 1992-10. Passages used: 'taking on a complex treatment of state formation, moral regulation, and the work of so-called voluntary reform organizations' (p. 315); 'to reshape the ethical subjectivity of both immigrants and native-born Canadians' (p. 316, quoting p. 17); the organizations studied (p. 316); '"the state has no monopoly on moral regulation" (p. 165)' (p. 317); 'a re-revisionist history of turn-of-the-century feminism' and 'not innocent of racism and classism' (p. 317); 'the social reform movements of the turn of the century helped to shape the bourgeoisie, which led the movements, as well as the working class' (p. 318, quoting p. 15); her reservations on 'not quite so sharply drawn' state and civil society and on moving 'quickly from analysis of discursive strategies ... to drawing conclusions about people's motives and intentions' (pp. 318–319).

new_sources.title: Chris McCormick, review of Mariana Valverde, The Age of Light, Soap, and Water, Atlantis 17, no. 2 (1992): 123–125.
new_sources.citation: Chris McCormick, review of Mariana Valverde, The Age of Light, Soap, and Water: Moral Reform in English Canada, 1885–1925 (Toronto, 1991), Atlantis 17:2 (Spring 1992): 123–125.

verification.note: Read in full in the journal's PDF (atlantisjournal.ca download 4199/3443; 3 pp.; signed Chris McCormick, Saint Mary's University). The journal page's citation metadata gives Atlantis 17:2, pp. 123–125, dated 1992-04-01; the first page begins with the end of Eileen Manion's preceding review, and a web search wrongly attributed this review to Manion. Passages used: 'historians cannot gather facts because facts, as well as the subjects who think they know them, are generated and given meaning in discourses' (p. 123, quoting the book's p. 9); a 'thorough' knowledge of context is 'optimistic' (p. 123); 'purity work was not simply a question of banning obscene books or suppressing prostitution but was rather a campaign to educate the next generation' (p. 124, quoting p. 17); 'Valverde does not use the word "control," but rather stresses how the processes she analyzes were part of a regulatory process. Regulation is a better word than control' (p. 124); 'an attempt at positive regulation, not simply repressive control' (p. 124).

lof_valverde_1991.note: For the 1.135 person entry. The book's pages were not read. Wording is known from (a) in-period reviewers' quotations, read: Dehli 1992 (pp. 15, 17, 165), McCormick 1992 (pp. 9, 17, 42, 43, 90), Loo 1992 (pp. 35, 36, 41, 164), Wright 1995 (pp. 9–13, 41, 42, 43, 89–90, 98, 103, 166); and (b) Google Books search-within snippets of the 2008 UTP reissue (volume ghqEyXf5950C), whose page images were not viewable. The reissue keeps the 1991 pagination for the original text: the snippets put the reviewers' pp. 15, 17, 165 and 166 on the same pages, and the 1991 preface's p. 9 at p. ix (so 1991 p. 10 = 2008 p. x). Crossref chapter records: Preface ix–xiv; Introduction to the 2008 Edition 1–14; 1. Introduction 15–33; Notes 168–201. Snippet wording used: 'Following but modifying Foucault's approach, I take the term "discourses" to refer not to language as separate from the real world but rather to organized sets of signifying practices' (p. x); 'Moral regulation is very closely linked to state formation, as the British school of historical sociology has argued; but as Foucault and his followers have pointed out, the state has no monopoly on moral regulation' (p. 165); moral regulation 'might be an important social process, which is intertwined with but is not an effect of either the economic or the political' (p. 165); 'Marxist accounts (and in Canada this chiefly means accounts produced by the political economy school)' (p. 165); 'one has to be sceptical of any claims that envision a clear separation between moral and economic regulation' (p. 166); n. 33 (p. 171) cites Valverde and Weir 1988; n. 34 (p. 171): in The Great Arch 'the role of the state in moral regulation is highlighted, and their theorization has been influential here; but the agencies of regulation internal to civil society are obscured'; n. 35 (p. 171) cites Bruce Curtis, 'Preconditions of the Canadian State'; p. 173: Corrigan and Sayer 'do not differentiate between moral and other modes of social regulation; by contrast, I restrict the term to mean the formation of ethical subjectivity'. The words before 'the term "moral regulation" from' on p. 173 were not visible. Acknowledgements (p. viii, snippet): 'Lorna Weir has been my best critic'.

pl129_valverde_1990.note: Re-read in full for the 1.135 person entry (lltjournal.ca article 4766, galley 5639). Page assignments from the running heads: 'the controversy about discourse theory' (p. 227); Scott's approach 'has much to commend it', her four elements 'somewhat arbitrary', 'transcending the idealism/materialism dichotomy' (p. 230); limitations 'symptomatic of the general limitations of discourse analysis as it has been used by social historians (myself included!)' (p. 231); 'an inherent bias in discourse analysis in favour of what some call "the sociology of domination." This problem, not discussed by Scott'; 'rather polemical book tends to sing the praises of discourse analysis without mentioning many of its problems'; 'the grandiose claim made by Scott on Foucault's behalf' (p. 232); 'she exaggerates the contribution Foucault and Derrida can make to historical work'; 'deserves to be carefully read even by those who find some of its more polemical claims hard to swallow' (p. 233).

cpl129_wright_1995.note: Valverde section re-read for the 1.135 person entry, pp. 122–126 (UNB PDF 12013/12857). Wright reviews The Age of Light, Soap, and Water as one of six books. Passages used: 'In her much talked about treatise'; the six authors include 'one a sociologist (Mariana Valverde)'; 'Following Foucault' (p. 122); 'Valverde is quick to avoid a "descent into discourse"'; she 'modifies Foucault's archaeology' and 'maintains an important commitment to social agency'; quotes the book's p. 43 on 'the decentring of the subject' (p. 123); quotes p. 166, '[m]oral regulation is an important aspect of ruling, helping to constitute class, gender, sexual, and race relations'; 'the concept of slippages', 'her most exciting, most original, contribution' (p. 124); her conclusion that audiences 'knew precisely what was meant' is 'untenable'; 'the impoverished immigrant and the "fallen woman" remain conspicuously silent' (p. 125); 'the silence of the consumer amidst the din of the producer gives the impression of top-down social control, precisely what Valverde sought to avoid' (p. 126).

crr_christie_gauvreau_1996.note: For the 1.135 person entry: Google Books search-within snippets (volume zcfujZowlDwC, partial preview; page images not viewed). Wording recorded but not page-image checked: 'historians such as Doug Owram and Mariana Valverde have adhered to a caricature of the antiquated and esoteric Victorian theologue to excise the churches from "progressive" currents of modern thought and social action' (p. xiii); 'Valverde has argued that in early twentieth-century Canada issues such as social purity and immigration were controlled by a hegemonic exercise of power by the state and middle-class organizations' (p. 187); 'Valverde's analysis wrongly posits the view that given the hegemonic influence of the state, there was only one option regarding immigration policy – that of racism and the annihilation of immigrant culture'; 'three divergent strands of opinion on the immigration question' (p. 188); n. 95 (p. 328) cites Valverde pp. 15, 112, 123–8 (and gives the subtitle's end date as 1914). Note 5 to p. xiii (p. 252) also discusses her book; its inner quotation ('are superseded by concerns about good citizenship and the imposition of bureaucratic and state control') was not found in her book by search and is not attributed to her.

cdnsrc_strange_loo_1997.note: For the 1.135 person entry: Google Books search-within snippets (volume lnKrT6fay9AC; page images not viewed). 'Theorists influenced by philosopher Michel Foucault have urged scholars to abandon the social-control model for a more flexible concept of regulation. Many scholars have accordingly tossed away the image of the hammer in favour of that of the net – restrictive, yet full of holes. Regulation theorists have also emphasized that state agencies and institutions are not the sole means by which behaviour is regulated' (p. 5); 'As Mariana Valverde and others have argued, Canadians, like their British and U.S. counterparts, inflated prostitution into the master problem of the age – "the social evil."' (p. 63). The further-reading list (p. 158) gives the 1991 book.

cdnsrc_hunt_1999.note: For the 1.135 person entry: Google Books search-within snippets (volume FD59ivQ8KxQC; page images not viewed). 'Valverde has argued that projects of moral regulation are not so much concerned with changing behaviour as with the ...' and 'I do not take issue with Valverde's invocation of ethical subjectivity, but I emphasise the mundane features of self-governing' (p. 155); 'Valverde is correct to identify moral regulation as being focused on the production of "ethical subjectivities" (Valverde 1991: 216)' (p. 189). Hunt's page reference 216 exceeds the 1991 book's 205 pages; unresolved.

cdnsrc_valverde_1998.note: For the 1.135 person entry: Google Books search-within snippets (volume Kl5ugmvDgH0C; page images not viewed). The introduction places liquor control where 'moral regulation, fiscal policy, and administrative law were mixed and managed with very little public input' (p. 9) and criticises studies that 'artificially isolate a single mode of governance, assuming that what is to be studied is medicalization, or professionalization, or the shift from disciplinary control to risk-based management' (p. 10; the words before were not visible). Not used as evidence for any edge.

cdnsrc_valverde_weir_1988.note: Still unread. Valverde's own 1991 note 33 (p. 171; Google Books snippet of the 2008 reissue) gives the subtitle as 'More Preliminary Remarks on Moral Regulation' (RFR 17, 3, September 1988, pp. 31–34); Weir's York profile gives 'Preliminary Remarks'. The 'More' would echo Corrigan's 1981 'Some Preliminary Remarks'. Not resolved; the title is left as it stands.
